![GLEN Appliances Targets 600–700 Exclusive Stores, Plans Offline Retail Push in West, South and East India ](https://indian-retailer.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/seoo%20images%20%2841%29.jpg)

From neighbourhood appliance stores to a larger manufacturing footprint, GLEN Appliances is preparing for its next phase of expansion in India. The homegrown kitchen and home appliances brand plans to expand its exclusive retail network from 236 GLEN Galleries to 500 over the next two years, with a longer-term ambition of reaching 600–700 outlets. Alongside its retail push, the company is doubling manufacturing capacity at its Faridabad facility to support growth across existing and new product categories.

Founded in 1999, GLEN recorded revenue of approximately Rs 440 crore in the previous financial year, according to Rintu Dasgupta, COO, GLEN Appliances. With a strong presence in North India, the company is now focusing on expanding across West, South and East India, while increasing its reach in Tier-II and Tier-III markets. It is also strengthening its online business and introducing new product categories as it looks to build a wider national presence. 

## Expanding the Exclusive Retail Network

GLEN's exclusive retail network is central to its plans to improve consumer access and strengthen its presence across India. The company currently operates 236 GLEN Galleries and aims to increase this to approximately 500 outlets over the next two years, eventually reaching 600–700 galleries nationwide.

The company opened around 36 galleries during the year up to the interview and expected to close the year with approximately 55–56 new outlets. While North India remains an important market, a larger share of incremental store additions is expected to come from West and South India, where the brand's existing gallery footprint is comparatively smaller.

“Most of the galleries currently getting opened are in South and West, mostly. The reason is that our gallery footprint today in these markets is pretty small,” said Rintu Dasgupta, COO, GLEN Appliances.

The company will continue to expand in North India as well, particularly in towns where it does not yet have a gallery. However, the region already accounts for a significant share of its established retail network.

GLEN Galleries follow a neighbourhood-store format, with outlets typically measuring between 250 and 350 sq. ft. Rather than prioritising large shopping malls, the company focuses on local markets and residential commercial complexes to remain accessible to consumers.

The stores operate through a franchise-led model. Franchisees purchase inventory, while GLEN provides the store branding, layout, furniture and fixtures.

“The franchisee has an equal say in the business as the brand, and he has significant skin in the game also, so that the stores remain operational till the time there is mutual benefit between the company and the franchisee,” Dasgupta added.

## Strengthening Presence Beyond North India

GLEN is looking to build on its established presence in North India by expanding distribution and retail access across western, southern and eastern markets. The company is also moving beyond the Tier-I urban centres that shaped its earlier growth, targeting smaller cities where rising income levels are creating opportunities for kitchen and home appliances.

“We are essentially an urban brand. In the initial part of the company's journey, we were essentially present in the Tier-I towns. Now, as income levels are increasing in Tier-II and Tier-III towns, our presence is also increasing in these towns,” Dasgupta said.

The company's distribution network includes approximately 350 distributors, supported by a sales team of around 180 people and nearly 370 service centres across India. Through this network, GLEN reaches consumers across approximately 5,500 multi-brand retail stores.

Beyond exclusive galleries and multi-brand outlets, the company also serves institutional customers and the Canteen Stores Department (CSD). Its modern trade presence remains limited, with a focus on B2B customers and selected regional retailers.

## Online Channels Contribute 17% of Revenue

While offline retail continues to account for most of GLEN's business, the company is strengthening its digital presence through its own website, e-commerce marketplaces and selected quick-commerce platforms.

Online channels contribute approximately 17% of the company's business, according to Dasgupta. Of this, around 14% comes from marketplaces and quick-commerce platforms, while its own website contributes approximately 3%. The remaining revenue comes from offline channels.

GLEN sells its full product range through Amazon and Flipkart, which Dasgupta identified as its largest e-commerce customers. Its presence on Swiggy Instamart, Blinkit and Zepto is more selective, focusing largely on entry-level, lower-priced products suited to impulse purchases.

The company is also taking a targeted approach to expanding its small-appliance business online. Rather than competing across the entire category, it intends to focus on product segments where it can offer the right combination of quality, features and pricing.

“We are not a price-driven brand in the market. We will never be a price-driven brand in the market. We are a brand which is razor-focused on quality,” Dasgupta said.

Categories such as OTGs and air fryers are among the products the company sees as suitable for online expansion. GLEN plans to concentrate on approximately six or seven large, growing categories where it believes it can offer differentiated products rather than spread its resources across the entire small-appliance market.

## Doubling Manufacturing Capacity in Faridabad

Manufacturing is another key component of GLEN's expansion plans. The company produces approximately 87–88% of the products it sells at its Faridabad facility, while the remaining share is imported. It is gradually looking to shift more of the imported product range to domestic manufacturing.

The existing facility was commissioned around 2020, following the company's move from its earlier factory in Faridabad's DLF industrial area. GLEN is now developing a new factory adjoining its current facility, with the aim of doubling manufacturing capacity within approximately a year of the interview.

“The reason that we are doing this is that we are very, very optimistic about the way the market is going to grow. The second is that our presence in this growing market will only get strengthened over a period of time,” Dasgupta shared.

The investment is intended to support the company's retail expansion and growing product portfolio while allowing it to retain greater control over manufacturing and quality.

Dasgupta said domestic manufacturing also provides an advantage in servicing products over their useful lives. Since the company controls production, it can maintain the availability of spare parts for its products for as long as consumers continue to use them.

“ As we manufacture ourselves, we exercise full control over the service and quality of the product,” he said.

## Chimneys and Cooktops Remain Core Categories

GLEN's product portfolio continues to be led by kitchen appliances, particularly chimneys, which account for approximately 40% of its sales. Cooktops and hobs together contribute another 22–23%, while built-in appliances, including ovens, microwaves and dishwashers, account for around 7–8% of total sales.

Over the past two years, the company has also entered new categories, including kitchen sinks, and is launching air purifiers and tabletop coffee machines. Its small-appliance range spans products such as mixer grinders, blenders, air fryers, water heaters and room heaters.

Although these newer categories are growing, they currently account for a smaller share of the company's overall business. Dasgupta expects them to make a more substantial contribution over the next three years as the portfolio expands.

The company is also investing in product innovation within its established categories. In chimneys, GLEN has moved from suction capacities of approximately 1,000–1,200 cubic metres per hour to models offering 1,400–1,600 cubic metres per hour, reflecting its focus on more effective smoke extraction and healthier kitchen environments.

“That's primarily to give a more efficient machine to the housewife, so that she can operate in a smoke-free environment in her house, and of course to launch more innovative products in the market,” Dasgupta said.

He added that the company is working on connected appliances, including products incorporating the Internet of Things (IoT), app-based functionality and design innovations. Several of these developments are expected to reach the market over the six to nine months following the interview.

## Building Market Share Through Quality and Service

GLEN aims to strengthen its market position over the next three to four years, with category-specific market-share targets guiding its expansion. The company is targeting approximately 15% market share in chimneys and around 10% in cooktops and hobs combined.

In small appliances, its focus is on building a profitable business while maintaining its mid-premium positioning. Rather than competing primarily on price, GLEN intends to concentrate on selected categories where product quality, design and service can differentiate its offerings.

The company plans to support these ambitions through continued investment in manufacturing, retail expansion, product innovation and after-sales service. Its priorities include maintaining product quality, ensuring spare-parts availability throughout a product's useful life and making its products accessible across a wider range of markets.

Dasgupta said the company's long-term approach is centred on creating a differentiated proposition for Indian consumers while sustaining growth.

“We want to grow at least 20 percent year-on-year and serve the customers as well as possible, and create a differentiated brand for the Indian market,” concluded Dasgupta.

![Kicky & Perky Targets 200 Stores in Three Years, Bets on Offline Retail to Drive Growth](https://indian-retailer.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/kicky.jpg)

Kicky & Perky is stepping up its retail expansion, targeting 200 stores over the next three years as the online-first jewellery brand looks to diversify its sales channels, strengthen customer engagement and build a scalable retail business. The company plans to open 20 stores over the next year before exploring franchising as a route to accelerate expansion.

The strategy marks a shift towards an omnichannel business model, with physical retail expected to play a larger role in customer acquisition, product discovery and revenue generation. The brand currently generates approximately 90% of its sales online and 10% offline, but aims to move towards a 70:30 offline-to-online sales mix over the longer term.

“Jewellery is a touch-and-feel product. Customers want to experience it before buying. With offline stores, we can explain the stories behind our collections and help customers understand the effort that goes into creating them,” said Rahul Agarwal, Business Head, Kicky & Perky.

**Offline Expansion Becomes a Key Growth Driver**

Kicky & Perky's retail strategy combines company-led store expansion with a data-driven approach to location selection. The brand is evaluating both shopping malls and high-street locations, with plans to assess their performance before committing to a preferred format.

According to Agarwal, the company considers three key factors when selecting locations: the concentration of its target customers, the positioning of neighbouring brands and insights from its online sales and conversion data.

“We evaluate where our target customers reside, which brands are located around us and what our online sales data tells us about customer acceptance and conversions. These three factors help us decide where to open our stores,” he said.

The brand's initial expansion is focused on Delhi and Mumbai, with Hyderabad, Bengaluru and selected markets in Punjab also on its radar. Pune and Varanasi are among the other cities being considered, particularly for their connection with art and culture.

The company sees different commercial advantages in mall and high-street retail. Malls offer access to established footfall, while high-street stores provide greater flexibility in storefront visibility and product presentation. Kicky & Perky plans to use its initial expansion phase to understand which format delivers better results for the business.

##### **Silver, Bridal Jewellery Offer Opportunities to Increase Average Selling Prices**

Alongside retail expansion, Kicky & Perky is looking to broaden its product mix across everyday jewellery, statement pieces and bridal collections. The strategy provides an opportunity to serve multiple purchase occasions while increasing the contribution of higher-value products.

The brand believes that changing consumer preferences are creating demand for versatile jewellery that can be worn across work, social gatherings and special occasions.

“Earlier, people would buy gold jewellery and take it out only for special occasions. Today, consumers want to accessorise themselves every day with pieces that enrich their overall look. They are also looking for jewellery that expresses their personality,” Agarwal said.

Bridal jewellery is emerging as another opportunity. Silver enables the brand to create elaborate, lightweight pieces, while gold-plated silver offers consumers an alternative to conventional gold jewellery.

“People want bridal jewellery that looks heavy but does not weigh heavily. They want to invest more in the look of the piece rather than the weight of the metal. Silver gives us the flexibility to create these designs,” Agarwal said.

The company is seeing opportunities in larger pieces such as Chandbalis, bridal sets and bridesmaid sets. These products carry higher average selling prices (ASPs) than smaller everyday pieces, potentially increasing revenue per transaction.

The brand is also expanding its range across categories such as hair accessories, nose pins and toe rings, creating additional opportunities to broaden its product portfolio and attract repeat purchases.

##### **Franchising to Support the Next Phase of Scale**

While Kicky & Perky intends to establish its first 20 stores through company-led expansion, franchising is being considered as a subsequent growth lever. Before bringing in partners, the company wants to establish standardised operating processes and test the economics of its retail model.

“We want to open the first 20 stores ourselves, test the model and establish processes that can withstand operational challenges. Once we are confident that the model is scalable, we will explore franchising with partners who understand what Kicky & Perky stands for,” Agarwal said.

This phased approach is intended to help the brand establish a replicable operating model before expanding through external partners. The company has not disclosed specific franchise investment requirements or store-level profitability targets.

##### **Quick Commerce and International Markets on the Roadmap**

Beyond physical retail, Kicky & Perky is exploring quick commerce as an additional distribution channel. The company plans to identify products suited to the channel, allowing it to reach customers seeking convenient access to jewellery.

International expansion is another part of its longer-term strategy. The brand aims to establish a global presence by building on India's strengths in gemstone availability and jewellery craftsmanship.

“Our aim is to become a successful Indian global brand. India has access to some of the best gemstones and artisans, and we want to build a brand that can represent that strength on the global stage,” Agarwal said.

The company has not disclosed its revenue targets in absolute terms but indicated ambitious growth expectations for FY2026–27 and the following financial year. Agarwal also emphasised that expansion would be guided by financial discipline rather than growth at any cost.

As Kicky & Perky pursues its 200-store ambition, execution will be critical. The company's ability to establish sustainable store economics, identify the right retail formats and build standardised operations will determine how effectively it can translate digital demand into a larger omnichannel business.

![Cura Targets Rs 500 Crore Revenue in 3 Years, Bets on Digital Expansion and Health Plus Range](https://indian-retailer.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/seoo%20imageee%20%2812%29.jpg)

Cura Ayurvedic & Unani Ltd. is preparing for its next phase of growth by expanding into digital commerce, developing new wellness products and strengthening its manufacturing capabilities. Founded by Hemant Sharma in 1999, the company reported revenue of Rs 107.18 crore in FY26, with a net profit margin of 30 percent. It is targeting Rs 500 crore in revenue over the next three years.

The company recently entered the direct-to-consumer (D2C) market and is expanding its presence on Amazon and Flipkart, with plans to enter quick commerce. It expects digital channels to contribute Rs 15–20 crore in their first full year.

For Aditya Mihir, Executive Director, Cura Ayurvedic & Unani Ltd., the expansion is not just about opening new sales channels. It is also about reaching consumers with relevant products while maintaining the relationships the company has built with offline retailers over the years.

“It's about reaching the right people for this. People who actually want to find a solution for their medical illness, rather than just buy a marketable product,” Mihir said.

## **Growing Online Without Losing the Offline Network**

Cura has built an offline distribution network spanning 17,000 pincodes across 28 states and eight Union Territories, according to the company. As it enters digital commerce, protecting this network remains an important consideration.

Mihir said the company had experimented with online sales three to five years ago but found that the channel was affecting its offline retailers. This prompted Cura to reconsider how it approached e-commerce before expanding its digital presence again.

“After two to three years of preparation and prep work, we have created the perfect combination to not cause even an inch of problem for our offline retailers,” he said.

The company is now looking to develop its online business while continuing to serve its established retail network. Its current priorities include expanding across marketplaces and preparing for quick commerce, with the Health Plus range expected to be an important part of its digital portfolio.

Cura expects its digital channels to generate Rs 15–20 crore in their first full year. The company is pursuing this alongside its overall revenue target of Rs 500 crore over the next three years.

## **Health Plus Leads the Next Product Push**

Product development is another focus as Cura looks to expand its presence in the wellness market. The company has 600 live SKUs across its portfolio and introduced Triphala Ras in 2006. It also works with more than 190 varieties of herbs, according to Mihir.

Its newer Health Plus range includes products focused on gut and liver health. Cura Gut Health Plus is among the products being introduced, while the company is also developing its liver-health offering. Further additions to the range will depend on consumer response and the company's assessment of market needs.

Explaining the thinking behind the portfolio, Mihir said the company was drawing on ingredients from different regions and the traditional knowledge associated with their cultivation.

“We are sourcing all the herbs and all the ingredients from that place directly,” he said.

The company expects the Health Plus range to contribute to its digital business as it expands online. Rather than relying solely on marketplace listings to drive growth, Cura is looking to use the channel to reach consumers for whom its products are relevant.

## **Manufacturing and Quality Control**

Cura's growth plans also include expanding its manufacturing footprint. The company currently has five manufacturing units and plans to establish two additional facilities in Jewar and Guwahati, according to information shared by the company. It also manufactures products for other wellness brands, including Kapiva.

Mihir said quality checks form part of the company's process, from the evaluation of incoming herbs to testing finished products. Cura has an internal quality assurance and quality control laboratory and works with third-party laboratories for testing, he said.

“At least, we do four quality tests. That is the bare minimum that we do. In some cases, it goes up to six to seven tests,” Mihir said.

He explained that ingredients are assessed against quality parameters before being used in production, while finished products undergo further checks before packaging and dispatch.

For certain herbal juice formulations, Mihir described a brewing process that runs continuously for 48 hours. The company also plans to make product-testing information more accessible to consumers through scannable QR codes, although this remains a future plan.

Cura has additionally stated that its five existing manufacturing units use solar energy and IGL, with no fossil fuel use reported across these facilities.

## **A Bootstrapped Approach to Growth**

Cura's expansion is being pursued without external funding, according to the company. Its plans combine investment in digital channels, product development and manufacturing with a continued focus on its existing distribution network.

Mihir said the company intends to grow through its own resources rather than seek external investment to accelerate expansion.

“We are not a brand which is looking for investors. We are not a brand which is looking for people to invest or to throw money at,” he said.

For the company, long-term consumer confidence is central to its ambitions. Mihir said Cura wants to build a brand that consumers can recognize and trust.

“We want to be the next startup of this category, where people trust the brand by its name,” he said.

With its digital business still at an early stage, Cura's next phase will depend on how effectively it expands online while maintaining its offline relationships. Its Health Plus portfolio, marketplace presence and planned manufacturing investments are expected to support this expansion as it works toward its Rs 500 crore revenue target over the next three years.

![Littlebox Plans EBOs across metros next year; Targets Rs 1000 Cr Turnover in 5 Years](https://indian-retailer.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/seoo%20imageee%20%285%29.jpg)

India’s fast-fashion market is seeing brands compete not only on pricing and design but also on how quickly they can identify trends, develop products, and bring them to consumers. For Littlebox, the answer lies in combining an online-first business model with control over manufacturing, technology-led production, and a product assortment that evolves every week.

Founded in 2022 by Rimjhim Deka Kakati and her husband, Partha Kakati, Littlebox has built its business around Gen Z consumers seeking access to global fashion trends at affordable price points. The brand currently sells exclusively through its own website and app, with no marketplace presence. As it prepares to enter offline retail, Littlebox is looking to extend its reach while retaining control over its customer relationships and product development.

“We wanted to cater to the Gen Z audience in the country. We could see that Gen Z consumers were very much exposed to all the trends happening around the world through social media. At Littlebox, we wanted to bring those fashion trends to them at an affordable and accessible price point,” said Rimjhim Deka Kakati, Co-Founder and CEO, Littlebox.

The company’s next phase of growth will focus on expanding its retail presence, strengthening its operating model, and increasing its share of consumers’ wardrobes. Over the next four to five years, Littlebox aims to become a Rs 1000 Cr brand in five years.

## **Building an Online-First Fashion Business**

Littlebox began in Guwahati, where the founders started operations from a rented one-bedroom flat with a small team. Having spent nearly a decade in fashion before launching the brand, Kakati brought experience in brand building, factory operations, and supply-chain management. The company established its manufacturing base in Delhi while maintaining offices in both Guwahati and Delhi.

The founders’ focus extended beyond creating a fashion label. They wanted to build a business with greater control over its distribution, production, and consumer insights. Littlebox remained bootstrapped until it raised its first round of funding in 2025, following which it began expanding more aggressively, according to Kakati.

From the outset, the brand chose a direct-to-consumer (D2C) model, selling exclusively through its own digital channels. This has allowed it to retain access to customer feedback and purchasing data while making decisions on product development, pricing, and assortment.

“From the very beginning, we have been selling through our website and app. We are not on any marketplaces, and we want the larger share of our sales to continue coming from our own app and website in the near future,” Kakati said.

She acknowledged that marketplaces can provide substantial sales volumes, particularly for young brands trying to establish themselves. However, Littlebox has prioritized direct consumer relationships over the additional reach that third-party platforms can offer.

“For me, it was very important that I know my consumers. I understand the data behind the purchases. I could analyze the data behind the transactions, which would help me take decisions. And then you control your price point at every step. There is a bigger control, a better decision-making capacity if you are on your own platform,” she said.

According to Kakati, the brand has seen consumers return to purchase through its own channels, reinforcing its decision to continue investing in the model. The objective is to build on this base rather than pursue marketplace expansion simply to increase volumes.

## **Relevance Over Exclusivity in Fast Fashion**

Littlebox primarily targets consumers aged 18 to 26, a segment that encounters fashion trends from different markets through social media and expects brands to respond quickly. In this environment, the company sees speed, affordability, and trend relevance as key factors in attracting repeat purchases.

Rather than positioning its products as designs unavailable elsewhere, Littlebox focuses on identifying emerging styles and making them accessible to its customers at the right time.

“I believe it is not about differentiation, but about how relevant you are for them,” Kakati said.

She explained that if a product such as a corset top gains popularity, the brand must ensure it reaches consumers while the trend is still relevant and at a price they can afford. This approach informs the company’s product-development cycle.

“In fast fashion, your whole idea is how fast you can make a product and bring it to your shelf, online or offline. At Littlebox, we launch around 150 products every week in order to maintain that freshness and relevance for the consumer,” she said.

The frequent launches are also intended to give customers reasons to return to the platform. Kakadi said the company regularly surveys consumers to understand what encourages them to shop with the brand again, with trend relevance emerging as an important response.

This model requires the brand to balance a constantly evolving assortment with the operational capacity to develop, produce, and launch products at speed.

## **Technology and Manufacturing at the Core**

Littlebox’s product-launch frequency is supported by its focus on managing the supply chain and integrating technology into production. The company handles its manufacturing process from the early stages, including raw-material procurement, and has built in-house systems to track consumer preferences, fabric performance, and emerging trends.

It also gathers customer feedback before developing product samples, using these insights to inform the assortment. This process allows the company to assess consumer interest before committing to production.

“We do not just work like a fashion brand where we spot a trend, make a product, and just go out there. We try to be very data-oriented. We also have a process where we take feedback from consumers even before making any sample,” Kakati said.

The company describes its model as real-time retail, with technology supporting both production planning and weekly launches. Kakadi said Littlebox maintains around 17 days of inventory stock, which she attributed to its technology-enabled operating system.

For the brand, the challenge has been to combine India’s established garment-manufacturing ecosystem with a more technology-led approach to fashion retail.

“India always had the manufacturing platform. There are so many export houses in India where we are manufacturing, and there are so many domestic brands. We had access to skilled laborers. Our job was to ensure that, as a modern, technology-first fashion company, we could marry technology with the supply chain,” she said.

By integrating consumer insights, product development, and manufacturing, Littlebox aims to shorten the gap between identifying a trend and making it available to customers. The model is central to its ability to introduce new products frequently without relying solely on seasonal collections.

## Offine Retail Expansion Plans

Although Littlebox has built its business entirely through digital channels, the company is preparing to enter physical retail. It plans to open around 30–40 stores across India in 2027, marking a significant step in its distribution strategy.

The initial expansion is expected to focus on markets where the brand already has a strong customer base. Delhi is likely to be the starting point, supported by the company's manufacturing presence in the region, before it expands into other parts of the country. The brand's existing order distribution provides a starting point for identifying potential markets. Delhi-NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad together account for around 50 percent of Littlebox's orders, while the remaining half comes from other markets, including Tier I and Tier II cities.

This distribution indicates that the brand's customer base extends beyond the largest metropolitan markets. Its planned stores will give the company an additional channel to reach consumers who currently shop through its website and app.

For Littlebox, offline expansion will add a new dimension to its existing model. While its current business allows it to control the digital shopping experience and access purchasing data directly, physical stores will extend the brand's presence into markets where consumers may prefer to discover and shop for fashion in person.

## **Rethinking Festive Demand**

Littlebox's approach to seasonal demand also reflects its focus on fast-moving trends rather than relying exclusively on traditional festive merchandising.

Kakati said the brand does not need to stock up specifically for Diwali in the way some other fashion retailers do. Instead, it adapts its marketing to the festive calendar while continuing to introduce products aligned with its core positioning.

The company's stronger months are generally December, January, and February, driven by occasions such as Christmas, New Year, and Valentine's Day. For the recent festive season, Littlebox introduced a collection that adapted Indian prints into Western silhouettes. The company also incorporated festive themes into its marketing and was working on a Halloween campaign.

However, the festive period creates operational challenges for its supply chain. Many of its textile and clothing manufacturers are based in Gujarat, where factory closures and labor shortages during festivals can disrupt production.

“The preparation for us is at the back end. Our supply chain gets disrupted because our vendors and clothing manufacturers are based in Gujarat, and there is a labor shortage as workers go home during festivals,” Kakadi said.

The brand therefore focuses on preparing for supply-chain interruptions while maintaining a relatively consistent customer-facing approach. Its festive collections are designed to fit its modern fashion positioning rather than shift entirely toward traditional occasionwear.

## **Building a Larger Share of Consumers' Wardrobes**

As Littlebox prepares to expand beyond its online-only model, its longer-term ambition is to become a regular destination for consumers shopping for dresses and other fashion products.

Kakadi recognizes that young consumers are unlikely to remain loyal to a single fashion brand. They experiment with different labels, silhouettes, and styles, creating an opportunity for retailers that can consistently offer relevant products.

“At Littlebox, it is important to understand how much of the wardrobe share we can take from our consumers. That is what we are focusing on from the consumer's point of view,” she said.

The ambition is to build repeat engagement by offering an assortment that evolves with consumer preferences, rather than depending on exclusivity or a limited set of signature products. Over the next five years, Littlebox aims to reach revenue of Rs 1,000 crore.

Achieving that scale will require Littlebox to sustain its product-launch pace, strengthen its supply-chain capabilities, and execute its planned offline expansion while continuing to grow its owned digital channels.

“As we expand into a larger retail business, our focus will remain on speed, consumer insights, and manufacturing control. These capabilities will be key to realizing our vision of building a Rs 1,000-crore fashion brand,” concluded Kakati.
